To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the Galena rock glacier is an ice-cored rock glacier, that the debris mantle is composed of coarse material that has been transported from the headwall by snow avalanches, and that the ice core is composed of 10 to12 percent debris.

the ice-cored rock glaciers of the Galena Creek area are composed of ice and debris, with a thin layer of debris on the surface, that are slow-moving, have low accumulation/ablation areas, and have a debris mantle that is not incorporated into the ice.
Galena Creek rock glaciers are unique in that they are ice-cored, and that their low ratio of accumulation to ablation areas results in slow movement and low sensitivity to climate.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
rock glaciers are not glaciers at all, but rather are large debris flows with an ice core.
the ice core is a major factor in the morphology and movement of rock glaciers.
ice-cored rock glaciers are very slow, very thin, and have very low accumulation rates, and are therefore very stable in a climatic sense.
The main takeaway from our work is that
rock glaciers are not simply a debris-covered glacier, but rather are a unique type of glacier that has a different response to climate change than a clean glacier.
ice-cored rock glaciers are not the same as clean glaciers, and should not be treated as such.
ice-cored rock glaciers are very common, and their presence should be considered in any study of mountain glaciation.
